decks.title: Motion in a Straight Line — Part 1: Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration
goals: Describe position along a straight line in a chosen frame of reference
Distinguish path length from displacement and speed from velocity
Use average and instantaneous velocity and acceleration, including as slopes and derivatives

slides.narration: A goods train, a delivery rider and a falling coconut all move, but to describe any of them we must first say where it is, measured from what, and in which direction. In this part we set up a position axis, separate the length of a path from the displacement, and meet velocity and acceleration as rates of change.

slides.heading: Frame of reference and position
slides.body_md: Motion is always described **relative to a frame of reference**: an origin, an axis and a clock.
bullets: Along a straight line we need one axis: choose an **origin** O and a **positive direction**.
The **position** x of a body is its signed distance from O; it is negative on the other side of O.
Moving the origin changes every position but not the separation between two positions.
A body at rest in one frame may move in another, so rest and motion are **relative**.

slides.narration: Pick an origin, such as a railway station, and a positive direction along the track. The position of anything is then its signed distance from the origin: positive on one side, negative on the other. Shift the origin and every position changes, but the gap between two positions stays the same. Whether something is at rest or moving also depends on the frame we choose.

slides.heading: Path length and displacement
slides.body_md: A body leaves O, goes to A and comes back to B.
bullets: **Path length** (distance): the total length of the route actually covered. It is a scalar and never decreases.
**Displacement** $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$: the signed change of position. It depends only on the end points, not on the route.
Always $|\Delta x| \le$ path length; they are equal only if the body never turns back.
Displacement can be positive, negative or zero; path length is never negative.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a delivery rider
slides.body_md: A delivery rider leaves a depot (the origin), rides 1200 m east to a shop and then 450 m back west to a customer. The trip takes 5 min 30 s ($= 330$ s). Find the path length, the displacement, the average speed and the average velocity.
bullets: Displacement $= x_\text{final} - x_\text{initial} = 750 - 0 = 750$ m, towards the east.
Average speed $= \dfrac{1650}{330} = 5.0$ m s$^{-1}$.
Average velocity $= \dfrac{750}{330} \approx 2.27$ m s$^{-1}$ east, smaller than the average speed.

Divide each by the three hundred and thirty seconds taken: the average speed is five metres per second, and the average velocity is a smaller number, about two point three metres per second eastwards.

visual.caption: Positions are signed distances from the origin.

slides.narration: Think about what depends on the choice of origin and what does not.

slides.heading: Average velocity and average speed
slides.body_md: Over a time interval from $t_1$ to $t_2$:
bullets: Average velocity carries a sign (its direction along the axis); average speed does not.
Average speed is never smaller than the magnitude of the average velocity.
After a round trip the average velocity is zero but the average speed is not.
SI unit of both: metre per second (m s⁻¹); 1 m s⁻¹ = 3.6 km h⁻¹.

headers: Can it be zero while the body moves?

visual.alt: Table comparing distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity: definition, sign and whether it can be zero for a moving body

slides.narration: Average velocity is displacement divided by the time taken, so it has a sign. Average speed is path length divided by the time taken, so it is never negative. Because the path is at least as long as the displacement, the average speed is never smaller than the size of the average velocity. After a full round trip the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero even though the body has been moving all the time.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two halves of a journey
slides.body_md: A bus on a highway covers the first half of the distance at $30$ km h$^{-1}$ and the second half at $45$ km h$^{-1}$. Find its average speed for the whole trip.
bullets: Take each half as $90$ km (any value gives the same answer). Time for the first half $= \dfrac{90}{30} = 3$ h; for the second half $\dfrac{90}{45} = 2$ h.
Average speed $= \dfrac{180}{3 + 2} = \dfrac{180}{5} = 36$ km h$^{-1}$.
Not the arithmetic mean $\dfrac{30 + 45}{2} = 37.5$ km h$^{-1}$: the bus spends more time at the lower speed.

visual.alt: Table of the two halves of a bus journey: distance, speed and time for each half and for the whole trip

slides.narration: Average speed is total distance over total time, not the average of the two speeds. Choose ninety kilometres for each half. The first half takes three hours, the second takes two hours, so one hundred and eighty kilometres take five hours: thirty six kilometres per hour. The simple mean of the speeds would give a larger answer, because the bus spends more time going slowly.

slides.heading: Instantaneous velocity: the slope of the tangent
slides.body_md: Shrink the interval: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$.
bullets: On an x–t graph the **chord** between two points has slope equal to the average velocity; the **tangent** at one point has slope equal to the instantaneous velocity.
The sign of v gives the direction; a steeper tangent means a larger speed.
Instantaneous speed is the magnitude |v|; a speedometer reads it.

functions.label: chord, t = 1 s to 3 s: slope 6 m/s
tangent at t = 3 s: slope 9 m/s

visual.alt: Position-time curve with the chord between one and three seconds, whose slope is the average velocity of 6 metres per second, and the tangent at three seconds, whose slope is the instantaneous velocity of 9 metres per second
visual.caption: The chord gives the average velocity over an interval; the tangent gives the velocity at one instant.

slides.narration: On a position time graph, the straight line joining two points, a chord, has a slope equal to the average velocity over that interval. Let the second point slide towards the first and the chord turns into the tangent, whose slope is the velocity at that instant. For this curve the chord from one to three seconds has slope six, and the tangent at three seconds has slope nine metres per second.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a particle that turns back
slides.body_md: A particle moves on the x-axis with $x = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t$ (x in m, t in s). For the interval 0 to 3 s find the velocity, the instants of rest, the displacement, the path length, the average velocity and the average speed.
bullets: Path length $= 5 + 1 + 5 = 11$ m (5 m forward, 1 m back, 5 m forward).
Average velocity $= \dfrac{9}{3} = 3.0$ m s$^{-1}$; average speed $= \dfrac{11}{3} \approx 3.67$ m s$^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Position-time graph of a particle that moves forward to 5 metres at one second, turns back to 4 metres at two seconds, then moves forward again to 9 metres at three seconds
visual.caption: The tangent is horizontal at the two turning instants.

slides.narration: Differentiate the position to get the velocity: six t squared minus eighteen t plus twelve. It vanishes at one second and at two seconds, which are the turning instants. The particle is at five metres after one second, back at four metres after two, and at nine metres after three. So it covers five metres forward, one back, five forward: eleven metres of path for a displacement of only nine.

slides.heading: Quick check: tangent and chord
slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.

functions.label: chord, t = 1 s to 3 s: slope 6 m/s
tangent at t = 3 s: slope 9 m/s

visual.alt: Position-time curve with the chord between one and three seconds, whose slope is the average velocity of 6 metres per second, and the tangent at three seconds, whose slope is the instantaneous velocity of 9 metres per second
visual.caption: The chord gives the average velocity over an interval; the tangent gives the velocity at one instant.

slides.narration: Remember which line on the graph gives the velocity at one instant.

slides.heading: Acceleration
slides.body_md: Average acceleration $\bar a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$; instantaneous $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$, the slope of the v–t graph.
bullets: SI unit: metre per second squared (m s⁻²); the sign shows the direction along the axis.
The body speeds up when v and a have the same sign, and slows down when they have opposite signs.
v = 0 at an instant does not mean a = 0: a ball at the top of its flight has v = 0 but is still being accelerated.
For Example 3, $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 12t - 18$: it is $-6$ m s$^{-2}$ when $v = 0$ at $t = 1$ s, zero at $t = 1.5$ s where $v$ is least ($-1.5$ m s$^{-1}$).

visual.alt: Velocity-time graph of the same particle: the velocity falls from 12 metres per second, crosses zero at one second, reaches a minimum of minus 1.5 metres per second at 1.5 seconds and rises again, crossing zero at two seconds
visual.caption: The slope of this graph is the acceleration; it is zero at the minimum.

slides.narration: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, the slope of the velocity time graph. When velocity and acceleration point the same way the body speeds up; when they point opposite ways it slows down. Notice on this graph that the velocity is zero at one second, yet the slope there is not zero: the particle is momentarily at rest but its velocity is still changing.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a metro train
slides.body_md: A metro train on a straight track speeds up from $18$ km h$^{-1}$ to $72$ km h$^{-1}$ in $6$ s. Find its average acceleration in m s$^{-2}$.
bullets: $\bar a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{20 - 5}{6} = 2.5$ m s$^{-2}$.

visual.alt: Table converting speeds between kilometres per hour and metres per second

slides.narration: Convert the speeds to metres per second first: eighteen kilometres per hour is five metres per second, and seventy two is twenty. The change in velocity is fifteen metres per second in six seconds, so the average acceleration is two and a half metres per second squared.

slides.heading: Speed and velocity at a glance
slides.body_md: Scalar and vector quantities along a line:
columns:
**Scalar-like (no direction)**
- Distance (path length)
- Average speed
- Instantaneous speed |v|
- Never negative

**Signed (direction by sign)**
- Displacement
- Average velocity
- Instantaneous velocity
- Acceleration

headers: Can it be zero while the body moves?

visual.alt: Table comparing distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity: definition, sign and whether it can be zero for a moving body

slides.narration: In straight line motion, direction is carried by a plus or minus sign. Distance and speed have no direction and are never negative. Displacement, velocity and acceleration are signed. For instantaneous values over a very short interval, speed equals the size of the velocity, but for longer intervals average speed can be larger than the size of the average velocity.

slides.heading: Quick check: zero velocity
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason.

visual.alt: Velocity-time graph of the same particle: the velocity falls from 12 metres per second, crosses zero at one second, reaches a minimum of minus 1.5 metres per second at 1.5 seconds and rises again, crossing zero at two seconds
visual.caption: The slope of this graph is the acceleration; it is zero at the minimum.

slides.narration: Look at the slope of the graph where the velocity touches zero.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Signed distance from the chosen origin
v = dx/dt: slope of the x–t tangent
a = dv/dt: slope of the v–t graph
Same sign: speeding up; opposite: slowing down

visual.alt: Summary table of position, displacement, velocity, speed and acceleration

slides.narration: To sum up. Position is a signed distance from an origin. Displacement is the change of position and is never longer than the path. Average velocity is displacement over time; average speed is path length over time. Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the position time graph, and acceleration is the slope of the velocity time graph. If velocity and acceleration have the same sign, the body speeds up.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: State the positive direction before writing a sign; give the direction with every displacement or velocity.
For average speed over two stages use total path ÷ total time, never the mean of two speeds.
Convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ (divide by 3.6) before using g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Find turning points from v = 0 before computing path length.

rows: about to move or to turn round

visual.alt: Table of the signs of velocity and acceleration and whether the body is speeding up or slowing down

slides.narration: Always state your positive direction, and give a direction with every displacement and velocity. For two stage journeys, divide the total path by the total time. Convert kilometres per hour to metres per second before mixing with other units. And to find the path length of a particle that may turn back, first find where its velocity is zero.

slides.narration: Many motions have an acceleration that stays constant, a car pulling away smoothly or a stone falling from a bridge. For these we can write simple equations that connect position, velocity, acceleration and time. We derive them two ways, apply them to falling bodies and to stopping a vehicle, and finish by reading motion graphs.

slides.heading: The equations of uniformly accelerated motion
slides.body_md: For constant acceleration $a$, initial velocity $u$, final velocity $v$, displacement $s$ in time $t$:
bullets: Choose the equation that **lacks** the quantity you neither know nor want.
A useful fourth form: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ (average velocity × time).
They hold only while the acceleration is constant; for a changing acceleration, integrate.
Signs matter: take one direction as positive and use signed u, v, a and s.

rows: s = u t + ½ a t²

visual.alt: Table of the equations for uniformly accelerated motion, the variable each lacks and when to use it

slides.narration: Here are the three equations of motion for constant acceleration. The first has no displacement in it, the second has no final velocity, and the third has no time. Pick the one that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor want. They only hold while the acceleration is constant, and every quantity carries a sign.

slides.heading: Deriving the equations from the v–t graph
slides.body_md: Constant acceleration makes the v–t graph a straight line from $u$ to $v$.
bullets: Slope $= a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, so $v = u + at$.
Area under the line = displacement = rectangle + triangle $= ut + \tfrac{1}{2}(v - u)t = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.
The same area is $\tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)t$; eliminate $t = \dfrac{v-u}{a}$ to get $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
Check with the picture: u = 4 m s⁻¹, v = 16 m s⁻¹, t = 6 s gives a = 2 m s⁻² and s = 60 m.

slides.narration: The slope of the line is the acceleration, so the final velocity is the initial velocity plus acceleration times time. The area under the line is the displacement. It splits into a rectangle of height u and a triangle on top, and adding them gives u t plus a half a t squared. Eliminating the time between the first two results gives v squared equals u squared plus two a s.

slides.heading: Deriving the equations by calculus
slides.body_md: Start from $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$ with $a$ constant and integrate.
bullets: Write $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$, so $a\,dx = v\,dv$; integrating from $x_0$ to $x$ gives $a(x - x_0) = \tfrac{1}{2}(v^2 - u^2)$.
If a depends on time, say a = 6 − 2t, the same steps give v and x without the constant-acceleration formulae.

rows: x = x₀ + u t + ½ a t²

visual.alt: Table showing how the equations of uniformly accelerated motion follow by integrating the constant acceleration

slides.narration: Calculus gives the same equations. Integrate acceleration with respect to time to get velocity, and integrate velocity to get position. For the third equation, write acceleration as v times dv by dx, rearrange to a d x equals v d v, and integrate. If the acceleration changes with time, this method still works, but the three formulae do not.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a metro leaves the station
slides.body_md: A metro train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $1.2$ m s$^{-2}$ until it reaches $72$ km h$^{-1}$. Find the time taken and the distance covered.
bullets: $t = \dfrac{v - u}{a} = \dfrac{20 - 0}{1.2} \approx 16.7$ s.
$s = \dfrac{v^2 - u^2}{2a} = \dfrac{400}{2.4} \approx 167$ m.
Check: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t \approx \tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 16.67 \approx 167$ m.

visual.alt: Table converting speeds between kilometres per hour and metres per second

slides.narration: First convert seventy two kilometres per hour to twenty metres per second. The time is the change in velocity over the acceleration, twenty over one point two, about sixteen point seven seconds. The distance is twenty squared over two times one point two, about one hundred and sixty seven metres. The average velocity times time gives the same distance, a useful check.

slides.heading: Quick check: choosing an equation
slides.body_md: Choose the equation that leaves out the unknown you do not need, then compute.

rows: s = u t + ½ a t²

slides.narration: Write down what you know, then choose the equation without the quantity you do not need.

slides.heading: Free fall and g
slides.body_md: Near the Earth's surface, with air resistance negligible, every body falls with the same downward acceleration $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.
bullets: Free fall means only gravity acts: a body dropped, thrown up or thrown down has the same acceleration.
Dropped from rest: $v = gt$, $y = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = 2gy$; successive distances in equal seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …
Heavy and light bodies reach the ground together in a vacuum; a feather lags in air only because of air resistance.
Take up as positive for a throw upward: then a = −g (and for a drop, with down positive, a = +g).

slides.narration: Take downward as positive, with the initial velocity zero. The height is half g t squared: half of nine point eight times nine, which is forty four point one metres. The speed at impact is g times t, twenty nine point four metres per second, which is over a hundred kilometres per hour.

slides.heading: Going up and coming down
slides.body_md: A ball thrown straight up at $u$: take upward as positive, so $a = -g$ throughout.
bullets: Rises for $t_\text{up} = \dfrac{u}{g}$ to a height $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$; at the top $v = 0$ but $a = -g$.
It returns to the launch height after $2u/g$ with speed $u$ downward: equal times up and down, equal speeds at equal heights.
Position $y = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ is a symmetric arch; velocity $v = u - gt$ is a single straight line of slope $-g$.

visual.alt: Height-time graph of a ball thrown straight up at 19.6 metres per second: a symmetric arch with the top at 2 seconds and 19.6 metres, back at the starting height at 4 seconds
visual.caption: Symmetric arch: equal times up and down.

slides.narration: Throw a ball upward and take up as positive. Its acceleration is minus g all the way, on the way up, at the very top and on the way down. The height against time graph is a symmetric arch, so the climb takes exactly as long as the descent, and the ball comes back to the launch height with the speed it started with.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a ball thrown upward
slides.body_md: A ball is thrown straight up at $19.6$ m s$^{-1}$ ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$). Find the time to the top, the maximum height, the total time of flight, and its height and velocity at $t = 3$ s.
bullets: Time of flight $= 2 \times 2 = 4$ s; it lands with speed $19.6$ m s$^{-1}$ downward.
At $t = 3$ s: $y = 19.6 \times 3 - \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9.8 \times 9 = 14.7$ m and $v = 19.6 - 9.8 \times 3 = -9.80$ m s$^{-1}$ (moving down, 1 s after the top).

visual.alt: Velocity-time graph of the same ball: a straight line of constant slope minus 9.8 metres per second squared, from plus 19.6 down to minus 19.6 metres per second
visual.caption: One straight line: the acceleration is −9.8 m s⁻² throughout, up and down.

slides.narration: The ball rises for twenty over nine point eight, which is two seconds, and reaches a height of nineteen point six metres. The whole flight takes four seconds. After three seconds it is on the way down, fourteen point seven metres up, and its velocity is minus nine point eight metres per second, exactly what we expect one second after the top.

slides.heading: Stopping distance and reaction time
slides.body_md: A driver sees danger, reacts, then brakes: **stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance**.
bullets: Reaction distance $= v t_r$: the car moves at steady speed $v$ during the reaction time $t_r$ (about 0.2 s to 1 s).
Braking distance $= \dfrac{v^2}{2a}$ for uniform deceleration $a$: it grows with the **square** of the speed.
Doubling the speed doubles the reaction distance but multiplies the braking distance by 4.
Reaction time can be measured by catching a dropped ruler: $t = \sqrt{2d/g}$ for a fall of $d$.

slides.narration: Stopping a car has two parts. During the driver’s reaction time the car keeps going at its full speed, and the distance is speed times reaction time. Then the brakes slow it, and the braking distance is v squared over two a. Double the speed and the braking distance becomes four times as long. That is why speed limits matter near schools.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: stopping from 72 km/h
slides.body_md: A car at $72$ km h$^{-1}$ ($20$ m s$^{-1}$) has a driver with reaction time $0.6$ s, and the brakes give a deceleration of $5$ m s$^{-2}$. Find the stopping distance. What if the speed were doubled?
bullets: Reaction distance $= vt_r = 20 \times 0.6 = 12$ m.
Braking distance $= \dfrac{v^2}{2a} = \dfrac{400}{10} = 40$ m.
Stopping distance $= 12 + 40 = 52$ m.
At $40$ m s$^{-1}$: $24 + 160 = 184$ m, about 3.5 times as much.

slides.heading: Reading motion graphs: slope and area
slides.body_md: A graph is a picture of the motion: read **slopes** and **areas**.
bullets: x–t graph: slope = velocity; horizontal = at rest; straight = uniform velocity; curved = changing velocity.
v–t graph: slope = acceleration; area (signed) between the curve and the t-axis = displacement; area above the axis counts forward, below counts backward.
a–t graph: area (signed) = change in velocity.

slides.narration: On a position time graph, the slope is the velocity: a horizontal line means rest, a straight sloping line means constant velocity, and a curve means the velocity is changing. On a velocity time graph the slope is the acceleration and the signed area under the curve is the displacement. Area above the axis counts forwards and area below counts backwards.

slides.heading: Worked example 9: a car on a straight road
slides.body_md: A car's velocity rises uniformly from 0 to $20$ m s$^{-1}$ in $10$ s, stays constant for $20$ s, then falls uniformly to zero in $5$ s. Find the accelerations, the distance covered and the average speed.
bullets: Accelerations (slopes): $\dfrac{20 - 0}{10} = 2.0$ m s$^{-2}$, then $0$, then $\dfrac{0 - 20}{5} = -4$ m s$^{-2}$.
Areas: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100$ m; $20 \times 20 = 400$ m; $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 20 = 50$ m.
Distance $= 100 + 400 + 50 = 550$ m; average speed $= \dfrac{550}{35} \approx 15.7$ m s$^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Velocity-time graph of a car on a straight road: a straight rise from zero to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds, a flat part to 30 seconds, then a straight fall to zero at 35 seconds
visual.caption: Three straight pieces: slopes +2.0, 0 and −4.0 m s⁻².

slides.narration: The three slopes are plus two, zero and minus four metres per second squared. The areas are a triangle of one hundred metres, a rectangle of four hundred metres and a triangle of fifty metres, so the car covers five hundred and fifty metres in thirty five seconds. Dividing gives an average speed of about fifteen point seven metres per second.

slides.heading: Worked example 10: velocity changes sign
slides.body_md: A trolley is pushed up a ramp at $6$ m s$^{-1}$ and has a constant acceleration of $-2$ m s$^{-2}$ along the ramp. Using the graph, find the displacement and the path length in the first $5$ s.
bullets: $v = 0$ at $t = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3$ s. Area above the axis: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 6 = 9$ m (up the ramp).
At $t = 5$ s, $v = 6 + (-2)(5) = -4$ m s$^{-1}$. Area below the axis: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 4 = 4$ m (down the ramp).
Displacement $= 9 - 4 = 5$ m; path length $= 9 + 4 = 13$ m.
Average velocity $= \dfrac{5}{5} = 1.0$ m s$^{-1}$; average speed $= \dfrac{13}{5} = 2.6$ m s$^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Velocity-time graph of a trolley that goes up a ramp and comes back: the line falls from 6 metres per second, crosses zero at 3 seconds and reaches minus 4 metres per second at 5 seconds
visual.caption: Area above the axis counts forward, area below counts backward.

slides.narration: The trolley slows, stops after three seconds, and then rolls back. The triangle above the axis is nine metres up the ramp. The triangle below the axis, from three to five seconds, is four metres back down. So the displacement is nine minus four, five metres, while the path length is nine plus four, thirteen metres.

notes.title: Motion in a Straight Line — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Frame of reference, position, path length and displacement
sections.body_md:
- Motion is described relative to a **frame of reference**. On a straight line we choose an **origin** and a **positive direction**; the **position** $x$ is the signed distance from the origin.
- Shifting the origin changes every position but not the **displacement** $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ (a signed quantity) nor the **path length** (the total length of the route, never negative).
- Always $|\Delta x| \le$ path length. For a rider who goes 1200 m east and 450 m back west, the path length is 1650 m and the displacement is 750 m east.
- A body at rest in one frame can be moving in another: **rest and motion are relative**.
- In this chapter bodies are treated as **point objects** moving along a straight line, so direction is given by the sign (+ or −).

key_terms.definition_md: A set of an origin, axes and a clock with respect to which positions and times are measured.
The signed change of position, final minus initial; it depends only on the end points.
The total length of the route actually covered; a scalar.

sections.heading: 2. Average and instantaneous velocity and acceleration
sections.body_md:
- **Average velocity** $\bar v = \Delta x/\Delta t$ (signed); **average speed** = path length $/\Delta t$ (never negative, and at least $|\bar v|$). For two equal distances at $30$ and $45$ km h$^{-1}$ the average speed is $36$ km h$^{-1}$, not the mean $37.5$.
- **Instantaneous velocity** $v = dx/dt$: the slope of the tangent to the x–t graph. Its magnitude is the instantaneous speed.
- **Acceleration** $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$: the slope of the v–t graph. Velocity and acceleration with the same sign: speeding up; opposite signs: slowing down. $v = 0$ at an instant does not imply $a = 0$.
- Example: $x = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t$ gives $v = 6t^2 - 18t + 12$, $a = 12t - 18$; the particle is at rest at $t = 1$ s and $2$ s. In 0 to 3 s its displacement is 9 m but its path length is 11 m.
- Conversion: 1 m s⁻¹ = 3.6 km h⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: The limit of Δx/Δt as Δt → 0, that is dx/dt.
The rate of change of velocity with time, dv/dt.

sections.heading: 3. Uniformly accelerated motion, free fall and stopping distance
sections.body_md:
- For constant acceleration: $v = u + at$, $\;s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, $\;v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (and $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)t$). Graphically: slope of the v–t line is $a$; the area under it is $s$ (a rectangle $ut$ plus a triangle $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$). By calculus: integrate $a = dv/dt$ once for $v$, twice for $x$; use $a = v\,dv/dx$ for $v^2$.
- Example: a metro train from rest at $1.2$ m s$^{-2}$ reaches $20$ m s$^{-1}$ in $16.7$ s after $167$ m.
- **Free fall:** only gravity acts, $a = g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$ downward for every body (air resistance neglected). Dropped from rest: $v = gt$, $y = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$; a stone dropped for 3 s falls 44.1 m and reaches 29.4 m s⁻¹.
- **Thrown upward** at $u$ (up positive, $a = -g$): time to top $u/g$, height $H = u^2/2g$, total time $2u/g$, returns with speed $u$. For $u = 19.6$ m s$^{-1}$: 2 s, 19.6 m, 4 s.
- **Stopping distance** = reaction distance $vt_r$ + braking distance $v^2/2a$. At 20 m s⁻¹, $t_r = 0.6$ s and $a = 5$ m s$^{-2}$ it is 52 m; doubling the speed makes it 184 m. A **reaction time** can be found from a dropped ruler: $t = \sqrt{2d/g}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Motion in which the acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction.
Motion under gravity alone, with a = g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward.

sections.heading: 4. Position–time and velocity–time graphs
sections.body_md:
- **x–t graph:** slope = velocity. Horizontal: at rest. Straight sloping line: uniform velocity (steeper = faster; downward slope = moving in the −x direction). Curve: changing velocity. A walker who goes at 3 m s⁻¹ for 20 s, rests 15 s and returns at 2 m s⁻¹ gives slopes +3, 0 and −2.
- **v–t graph:** slope = acceleration; the **signed area** between the curve and the t-axis = displacement. For path length, add the areas without signs. A car that speeds up to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s, cruises 20 s and brakes in 5 s covers $550$ m with accelerations $+2.0$, $0$ and $-4.0$ m s$^{-2}$.
- **a–t graph:** signed area = change in velocity.
- A trolley with $u = 6$ m s$^{-1}$ and $a = -2$ m s$^{-2}$: displacement 5 m, path length 13 m in 5 s (area above the axis 9 m, below 4 m).
- Graphs show how a quantity changes with time; they do not show the shape of the path. The equations of uniform acceleration cannot be applied across a point where the acceleration changes.

questions.stem_md: A passenger sits in a coach of a train moving steadily past a platform. She says the bag on the luggage rack is at rest; a porter on the platform says the same bag is moving. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Only the porter is right, because the platform is fixed to the ground
Both cannot be right; one of them has made a measuring error
The bag is at rest in every frame because nothing pushes it
Both are right: rest and motion are relative to the frame of reference chosen

questions.solution_md: Position is measured from an origin in a chosen frame. In the coach frame the bag does not change position; in the platform frame it does — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On a straight railway line a signal post is at x = +250 m and the front of a goods train is at x = +700 m. The origin is now shifted to the signal post, keeping the positive direction the same. The train front is then at

options.text_md: +950 m, and its distance from the signal becomes 950 m
+450 m, and its distance from the signal stays 450 m
+700 m, and its distance from the signal becomes 450 m
−450 m, and its distance from the signal stays 450 m

questions.solution_md: New position = old position − position of the new origin = 700 − 250 = 450 m. The separation of two bodies does not depend on the origin — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On a hill road a surveyor notes only the straight-line change of position of her jeep from the start to the end of the trip, together with its direction. This quantity is called the ___ of the jeep.
questions.solution_md: It is the **displacement**: final position minus initial position.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Between two instants, the magnitude of the displacement of a body can never be greater than the length of the path it covers in that interval.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The straight-line change of position cannot exceed the length of any route between the same two positions; the two are equal only if the body never turns back.

questions.stem_md: A lift in a Mumbai tower starts at the ground floor (height 0), rises 36 m to the terrace and then comes down to a landing 15 m above the ground. Taking up as positive, find the displacement of the lift from start to finish, in m.
questions.solution_md: $\Delta x = x_\text{final} - x_\text{initial} = 15 - 0 = 15$ m (upward). The path length is 36 + 21 = 57 m, which is larger.

questions.stem_md: A morning walker on a straight canal bank in Lucknow goes 640 m east, then 260 m west and finally 350 m east. Find the total path length covered, in m.
questions.solution_md: Path length $= 640 + 260 + 350 = 1250$ m. (Her displacement is only $640 - 260 + 350 = 730$ m east.)

options.text_md: +25 m and 85 m
−25 m and 85 m
+85 m and 25 m
+25 m and 25 m

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A porter who walks 120 m along a platform from a train door to the exit gate and then back to the same door has zero displacement.

**Reason (R):** Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions of the body, not on the route followed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, and R explains A: start and finish coincide, so Δx = 0 even though the path length is 240 m — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A coin lies on the floor of a coach moving steadily along a straight track. Describe the coin’s motion in two different frames of reference to show that rest and motion are relative.

answer.model_answer_md: For a passenger in the coach (frame fixed to the coach) the coin keeps the same position, so it is **at rest**. For a person on the platform (frame fixed to the ground) its position changes with time, so it is **moving** with the speed of the train. Motion has meaning only with respect to a chosen frame.

questions.solution_md: Coach frame: rest. Ground frame: moving.

marking_scheme.step: Coach frame: position unchanged, at rest
Ground frame: position changes, moving; so motion is relative

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between path length and displacement for a body moving along a straight line, and give one example in which the path length is more than the magnitude of the displacement.

answer.model_answer_md: **Path length** is the total length of the route covered, a scalar that is never negative. **Displacement** is final minus initial position: signed, and fixed by the end points only. Example: a lift rising 36 m and then coming down 15 m has path length 51 m but displacement 21 m upward.

questions.solution_md: Route length vs change of position; example with turning back.

marking_scheme.step: Path length: total route; displacement: final − initial position

questions.stem_md: A courier van covers the first half of a 180 km route at 45 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Find its average speed for the whole route, in km/h (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Each half is $90$ km. $t_1 = \dfrac{90}{45} = 2$ h and $t_2 = \dfrac{90}{60} = 1.5$ h. Average speed $= \dfrac{180}{2 + 1.5} = \dfrac{180}{3.5} \approx 51.4$ km/h (not the mean of 45 and 60).

marking_scheme.step: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time ≈ 51.4 km/h

questions.stem_md: A cyclist rides 3.0 km east in 10 min and then 1.0 km west in 5 min. Find the magnitude of her average velocity over the whole 15 min, in m/s (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Net displacement $= 3000 - 1000 = 2000$ m east; total time $= 15 \times 60 = 900$ s. $\bar v = \dfrac{2000}{900} \approx 2.22$ m/s (her average speed is larger: $4000/900 \approx 4.44$ m/s).

questions.stem_md: The position of a particle on the x-axis is x = 6t − 2t² + 0.5t³, with x in m and t in s. Find its velocity at t = 2.0 s, in m/s.
questions.solution_md: $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 6 - 4t + 1.5t^2$. At $t = 2$ s: $v = 6 - 4 \times 2 + 1.5 \times 4 = 4$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: For the same particle (x = 6t − 2t² + 0.5t³ in SI units), find its acceleration at t = 2.0 s, in m/s².

marking_scheme.step: a = dv/dt = −4 + 3t = 2 m/s² at t = 2.0 s

questions.stem_md: A particle moves along the x-axis with x = 6t − 2t² + 0.5t³ (SI units) for t ≥ 0. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text_md: It is momentarily at rest at t = 2 s
It is momentarily at rest at t = 4 s
Its acceleration is the same at all times
Its velocity is never zero, so it never turns back

questions.solution_md: $v = 6 - 4t + 1.5t^2$ has discriminant $16 - 36 < 0$, so $v$ never vanishes ($v(2) = 4$ m/s, $v(4) = 14$ m/s); $a = -4 + 3t$ changes with time — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A tram in Kolkata speeds up from 7.2 km/h to 36 km/h in 4.0 s along a straight street. Find its average acceleration, in m/s² (2 significant figures).
A truck moves east along a straight highway while its speed falls steadily as the driver brakes. The direction of its acceleration is

options.text_md: west, opposite to its velocity
east, along its velocity
zero, because it moves along a straight line
vertically downward

questions.solution_md: Velocity points east and its magnitude decreases, so the change in velocity (and hence the acceleration) points west — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The speedometer of a motorbike reads 48 km/h at one instant of a ride. This reading is the bike’s

options.text_md: instantaneous speed at that instant
average velocity over the last minute
displacement per hour since the start
acceleration at that instant

questions.solution_md: A speedometer shows the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, that is, the instantaneous speed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the average velocity of a body over some time interval is zero, its average speed over that interval must also be zero.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A body that returns to its starting point has zero displacement and so zero average velocity, but its path length, and hence its average speed, is not zero.

questions.stem_md: For a lift pulling away from the ground floor, the rate at which its velocity changes with time is called its ___.
questions.solution_md: The **acceleration**, a = dv/dt.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A body whose velocity is zero at some instant must also have zero acceleration at that instant.

**Reason (R):** Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, not of position.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: a stone thrown upward has v = 0 at the top but its velocity is still changing (a = 9.8 m/s² downward) — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The average acceleration of a body over an interval is its change in velocity divided by the length of the interval.

**Reason (R):** Acceleration is measured in metre per second squared in the SI system.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the unit of acceleration does not explain how it is defined — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On the position–time graph of a scooter moving along a straight road, the velocity of the scooter at t = 20 s is given by

options.text_md: the area under the curve up to t = 20 s
the height of the curve at t = 20 s
the slope of the chord from t = 0 to t = 20 s
the slope of the tangent to the curve at t = 20 s

questions.solution_md: Instantaneous velocity is dx/dt, the slope of the tangent at that instant; the chord gives only the average velocity over an interval — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Define instantaneous velocity and explain how it can be obtained from the position–time graph of a body moving along a line.

answer.model_answer_md: **Instantaneous velocity** is the limit of the average velocity Δx/Δt as the interval Δt tends to zero, that is **dx/dt**. On an x–t graph, the chord between two points gives the average velocity; as one point moves towards the other the chord becomes the **tangent**, whose slope at that point is the instantaneous velocity.

questions.solution_md: Limit of Δx/Δt; slope of tangent.

marking_scheme.step: Slope of the tangent on the x–t graph

questions.stem_md: Explain why the average speed of a body over an interval can be greater than the magnitude of its average velocity but can never be smaller.

answer.model_answer_md: Average speed is **path length ÷ time** and the magnitude of average velocity is **|displacement| ÷ time**. The path length is always at least as large as the magnitude of the displacement, so the average speed is never smaller. It is larger when the body turns back, and equal when it moves in one direction only.

questions.solution_md: Path length ≥ |displacement|.

marking_scheme.step: Path ≥ |displacement|; equal only without turning back

questions.stem_md: A ball thrown vertically upward has zero velocity at the highest point of its flight. Is its acceleration zero there? Explain, and state how the signs of velocity and acceleration show whether a body is speeding up or slowing down.

answer.model_answer_md: The acceleration is **not zero**: it is g = 9.8 m/s² downward, because the velocity is still changing; at the top the velocity merely passes through zero while changing from upward to downward. Along a line, a body **speeds up** when velocity and acceleration have the **same sign** and **slows down** when their signs are **opposite**; on the way up v is positive and a negative, so the ball slows down.

questions.solution_md: a = g at the top; sign rule.

marking_scheme.step: Acceleration is not zero: 9.8 m/s² downward at the top
Velocity is changing, only momentarily zero
Same sign: speeding up; opposite signs: slowing down

questions.stem_md: On a position–time graph of a car on a straight road, how would you find (a) its average velocity between two instants and (b) its velocity at one instant? Explain how (b) is the limiting case of (a).

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Join the two points on the curve by a **chord**; its slope Δx/Δt is the **average velocity** over that interval. (b) Draw the **tangent** at the point; its slope is the velocity at that instant. If the second point is brought closer to the first, Δt → 0 and the chord turns into the tangent, so dx/dt is the limit of Δx/Δt.

questions.solution_md: Chord vs tangent; limit Δt → 0.

marking_scheme.step: Average velocity = slope of the chord
Instantaneous velocity = slope of the tangent
Tangent is the limit of the chord as Δt → 0

questions.stem_md: A particle moves on the x-axis with x = t³ − 6t² + 9t (x in m, t in s). Find its average speed during the first 4.0 s, in m/s.
questions.solution_md: $v = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t-1)(t-3)$ vanishes at $t = 1$ s and $3$ s. $x(0) = 0$, $x(1) = 4$ m, $x(3) = 0$ m, $x(4) = 4$ m. Path length $= 4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ m (displacement only 4 m). Average speed $= \dfrac{12}{4} = 3$ m/s.

marking_scheme.step: Turning instants t = 1 s and 3 s; path length = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 m

questions.stem_md: A cart on a straight track starts from rest and has an acceleration a = 6 − 2t (SI units). Find its velocity at t = 2.0 s, in m/s.
For the same cart (a = 6 − 2t in SI units, starting from rest at x = 0), find its displacement in the first 3.0 s, in m.
A bus on a ghat road speeds up uniformly from 5.0 m/s to 15 m/s in 10 s. Find the distance it covers in this time, in m.
questions.solution_md: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{15 - 5}{10} = 1$ m/s$^2$. $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 5 \times 10 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 100 = 100$ m. (Check: $\tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 10 = 100$ m.)

questions.stem_md: A goods train running at 108 km/h is brought to rest in 750 m by uniform braking. Find the retardation, in m/s² (2 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $u = 108$ km/h $= 30$ m/s, $v = 0$. From $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$: $0 = 900 + 2a(750)$, so $a$ is negative (a retardation) and $|a| = \dfrac{900}{1500} = 0.60$ m/s$^2$. (The train stops in $\dfrac{1500}{30} = 50$ s.)

marking_scheme.step: 108 km/h = 30 m/s; v² = u² + 2as with v = 0

questions.stem_md: A car starts from rest on a straight road with a constant acceleration of 1.8 m/s². Find the distance it covers during the fifth second of its motion (between t = 4 s and t = 5 s), in m.
questions.solution_md: With $u = 0$, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. $s(5) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.8 \times 25 = 22.5$ m and $s(4) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.8 \times 16 = 14.4$ m. Distance in the fifth second $= 22.5 - 14.4 = 8.1$ m.

questions.stem_md: A coconut drops from a palm 12.0 m above the ground. Neglecting air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), find its speed just before it hits the ground, in m/s (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: From rest, $v^2 = 2gh = 2 \times 9.8 \times 12 = 235.2$, so $v = \sqrt{235.2} \approx 15.3$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: A fielder throws a cricket ball vertically upward at 24.5 m/s. Neglecting air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), find the maximum height it reaches above the point of release, in m (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: At the top $v = 0$, so $0 = u^2 - 2gH$ and $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g} = \dfrac{600.25}{19.6} \approx 30.6$ m.

questions.stem_md: A student drops a ruler without warning and a partner catches it after it has fallen 0.18 m. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², find the partner’s reaction time, in s (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The ruler falls from rest: $d = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, so $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2d}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 0.18}{9.8}} \approx \sqrt{0.0367} \approx 0.192$ s.

questions.stem_md: A car moving at 54 km/h on a straight road has a driver whose reaction time is 0.80 s; after that the brakes give a uniform deceleration of 5.0 m/s². Find the total stopping distance, in m.
questions.solution_md: $54$ km/h $= 15$ m/s. Reaction distance $= vt_r = 15 \times 0.8 = 12$ m. Braking distance $= \dfrac{v^2}{2a} = \dfrac{225}{10} = 22.5$ m. Stopping distance $= 12 + 22.5 = 34.5$ m.

questions.stem_md: A ball is dropped from the top of an 80 m tower. At the same instant a second ball is thrown vertically upward from the foot of the tower at 40 m/s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², after how many seconds are the two balls at the same height?
questions.solution_md: Heights above the ground: $y_1 = 80 - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ and $y_2 = 40t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Setting $y_1 = y_2$ the $g$ terms cancel: $80 = 40t$, so $t = \dfrac{80}{40} = 2$ s. (They meet at a height of $80 - 4.9 \times 4 = 60.4$ m.)

questions.stem_md: A car passes a stationary police motorcycle on a straight road at a constant 20 m/s. At that instant the motorcycle starts from rest with a constant acceleration of 2.5 m/s². After how many seconds does it catch up with the car?
questions.solution_md: Car: $x_1 = 20t$. Motorcycle: $x_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2.5\,t^2 = 1.25t^2$. Setting $x_1 = x_2$: $20t = 1.25t^2$, so $t = \dfrac{20}{1.25} = 16$ s, when each has covered $320$ m (the motorcycle is then going at $40$ m/s).

questions.stem_md: A ball is dropped from a bridge. The distances it falls in the first, second and third seconds are in the ratio
questions.solution_md: Total fall $\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ is in the ratio $1 : 4 : 9$ after 1, 2 and 3 s, so the distances in successive seconds are $1 : 3 : 5$ (4.9 m, 14.7 m, 24.5 m) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A car brakes on a dry road with the same deceleration at every speed. If it brakes from twice the speed (ignoring reaction time), its braking distance becomes

options.text_md: twice as long
half as long
four times as long
eight times as long

questions.solution_md: From $v^2 = 2as$, the braking distance $s = \dfrac{u^2}{2a}$ is proportional to $u^2$; doubling $u$ gives four times the distance — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a vacuum chamber a brick and a marble are released together from the same height. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Both reach the floor together, because they have the same mass
The brick reaches first, because gravity pulls harder on it, so it accelerates more
Both reach the floor together, because both have the same acceleration g
The marble reaches first, because it is smaller

questions.solution_md: Without air resistance, the only force is gravity; the force on the brick is larger but so is its mass, so every body has the same acceleration g — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A stone thrown vertically upward passes a window 6 m above the thrower on the way up and again on the way down. Neglecting air resistance, its speed at the window on the way down, compared with its speed at the window on the way up, is

options.text_md: larger, because it has been speeding up since the top
smaller, because it has lost energy
the same in magnitude
zero

questions.solution_md: The motion is symmetric about the top: at the same height the speed is the same going up and coming down, only the direction differs — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 14.7 m/s and caught at the level of release. With g = 9.8 m/s² and no air resistance, the time it spends in the air is
questions.solution_md: Time to rise $= \dfrac{u}{g} = \dfrac{14.7}{9.8} = 1.5$ s, and the fall takes the same time: $2 \times 1.5 = 3.0$ s — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A scooter moving at 25 m/s is braked uniformly and stops in 62.5 m. To find the retardation directly, without first finding the time, the most suitable equation is

options.text_md: v = u + at
v² = u² + 2as
s = ut + ½at²
s = ½(u + v)t

questions.solution_md: The data are $u$, $v = 0$ and $s$; time is neither given nor needed, so use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (this gives $a = -\dfrac{625}{125} = -5$ m/s$^2$) — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A coin dropped from a balcony gains a speed of about 9.8 m/s in every second of its fall (air resistance neglected).

**Reason (R):** The distances fallen by the coin in successive seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. A follows from a = g = 9.8 m/s² (so v = gt), whereas R describes the distances, which does not explain the gain of speed — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ball thrown vertically upward takes as long to reach its highest point as it takes to fall back to the point of throw (air resistance neglected).

**Reason (R):** The ball’s acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downward at every instant of its flight.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: with constant a = −g, v = u − gt reaches zero at t = u/g, and the descent is the mirror image of the climb — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For a stone dropped from a tower (air resistance neglected), its constant downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s² is called the acceleration due to ___.
questions.solution_md: The acceleration due to **gravity**, g.

questions.stem_md: A coin and a feather are released together in a long glass tube, first with air in it and then after the air has been pumped out. Compare the two falls and state the value of g used.

answer.model_answer_md: With **air** in the tube the feather lags, because air resistance is large compared with its tiny weight. With the air **pumped out** only gravity acts, so both have the same acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² downward and land together; the difference was caused by air resistance, not by gravity.

questions.solution_md: Air resistance causes the lag; in vacuum both have g.

marking_scheme.step: Air: feather lags because of air resistance
Vacuum: same acceleration g = 9.8 m/s², land together

questions.stem_md: Why does a car travelling twice as fast need much more than twice the distance to stop? Use the two parts of the stopping distance.

answer.model_answer_md: Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. The **reaction distance** v t_r is proportional to v, so it doubles. The **braking distance** v²/2a is proportional to v², so it becomes **four times** as large. The sum therefore grows by more than a factor of two.

questions.solution_md: Reaction part doubles; braking part quadruples.

marking_scheme.step: Braking distance ∝ v²: four times, so total more than doubles

questions.stem_md: Describe how a ruler dropped between a classmate’s fingers can be used to estimate her reaction time, and write the formula used.

answer.model_answer_md: Hold the ruler so its zero mark is level with her open fingers, release it without warning, and note the distance d it falls before she grips it. The ruler falls freely from rest, so d = ½gt², giving the **reaction time t = √(2d/g)**; a longer fall means a slower reaction.

questions.solution_md: Free fall from rest, t = √(2d/g).

marking_scheme.step: Drop the ruler without warning; note the distance d caught

questions.stem_md: Using the velocity–time graph of a body moving with constant acceleration a from velocity u to velocity v in time t, derive v = u + at and s = ut + ½at².

answer.model_answer_md: The graph is a straight line from u to v. Its **slope** is a = (v − u)/t, so **v = u + at**. The **area** under it is the displacement s: a rectangle of height u and width t, giving ut, plus a triangle of height (v − u) = at and base t, giving ½at·t. Hence **s = ut + ½at²**.

questions.solution_md: Slope gives v = u + at; area gives s.

marking_scheme.step: Slope of the v–t line: a = (v − u)/t, so v = u + at
Area = rectangle ut + triangle ½(v − u)t
(v − u) = at, so s = ut + ½at²

questions.stem_md: Starting from a = dv/dt, show by calculus that a body with constant acceleration a obeys v² = u² + 2as, where s is its displacement.

answer.model_answer_md: Write a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = **v dv/dx**, so a dx = v dv. Integrate from the start (position x₀, velocity u) to the end (position x, velocity v) with a constant: **a(x − x₀) = ½(v² − u²)**. With s = x − x₀ this gives **v² = u² + 2as**.

questions.solution_md: a = v dv/dx, integrate.

marking_scheme.step: a = dv/dt = v dv/dx, so a dx = v dv
Integrate with constant a between the limits
a s = ½(v² − u²), hence v² = u² + 2as

questions.stem_md: A driver brakes after seeing a hazard. Explain how the stopping distance of the car depends on its speed, the driver’s reaction time and the braking deceleration.

answer.model_answer_md: Stopping distance = **reaction distance** + **braking distance**. In the reaction time t_r the car moves at steady speed v, covering v t_r, so a slower driver adds distance in proportion to both v and t_r. After that the brakes give deceleration a, and the car travels **v²/2a**: this grows with the square of v and falls as a increases (a better road or tyres).

questions.solution_md: v t_r + v²/2a.

marking_scheme.step: Stopping distance = reaction distance v t_r + braking distance
Braking part v²/2a ∝ v², smaller for larger a

questions.stem_md: On the position–time graph of an auto-rickshaw parked outside a station, the line drawn for the auto is horizontal, parallel to the time axis. This shows that

options.text_md: it moves with a constant velocity
its position does not change with time: it is at rest
it moves with a constant acceleration
its velocity is increasing steadily

questions.solution_md: The slope of an x–t graph is the velocity; a horizontal line has zero slope, so the velocity is zero and the position is constant — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The velocity–time graph of a metro train between two stations is a trapezoid: a straight rise from 0 to 16 m/s in 8 s, a horizontal line for 40 s, then a straight fall to zero in 12 s. Find the distance between the stations, in m.
questions.solution_md: Distance = area under the graph. Rising part: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 16 = 64$ m; steady part: $16 \times 40 = 640$ m; falling part: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 16 = 96$ m. Total $= 64 + 640 + 96 = 800$ m.

questions.stem_md: For the same metro train (speed 16 m/s falling uniformly to zero in the last 12 s), find the magnitude of the retardation during the last 12 s, in m/s² (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The magnitude of the slope of the falling line is $\left|\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\right| = \dfrac{16}{12} \approx 1.33$ m/s$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist’s position–time graph on a straight road is drawn in four different ways (Column A). Match each drawing with what the cyclist is doing (Column B).

options.text_md: A straight line sloping upward
A horizontal straight line
A curve that gets steeper with time
A straight line sloping downward

questions.solution_md: The slope of an x–t graph is the velocity: positive constant slope — uniform velocity along +x; zero slope — rest; slope increasing — speeding up; negative constant slope — uniform velocity along −x.

questions.stem_md: A ball rolling in a straight groove has velocity +8.0 m/s at t = 0 and a constant acceleration of −2.5 m/s² (SI units). Using the v–t graph, find its displacement in the first 6.0 s, in m.
questions.solution_md: $v = 0$ at $t = \dfrac{8.0}{2.5} = 3.2$ s; area above the axis $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3.2 \times 8.0 = 12.8$ m. At $t = 6$ s, $v = 8.0 - 2.5 \times 6 = -7$ m/s; area below the axis $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2.80 \times 7 = 9.80$ m. Displacement $= 12.8 - 9.80 = 3.00$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Area above the axis 12.8 m (0 to 3.2 s)

questions.stem_md: A toy car starts from rest and its velocity–time graph is a straight line through the origin. Its position–time graph is

options.text_md: a straight line through the origin
a horizontal line
a curve that gets less steep with time
a curve that gets steeper with time, starting with zero slope

questions.solution_md: A straight v–t line through the origin means $v = at$, so $x = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: a parabola whose slope $v$ keeps increasing from zero — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The velocity–time graph of a trolley is a straight line that slopes downward but stays above the time axis for the whole time of interest. The trolley is

options.text_md: moving in the negative direction while speeding up
at rest
moving in the positive direction while slowing down, with constant negative acceleration
moving in the positive direction while speeding up

questions.solution_md: v stays positive, so it moves in the +x direction; the slope (acceleration) is negative and constant, and v decreases, so it slows down — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The area between an acceleration–time graph and the time axis gives the change in velocity of the body.

**Reason (R):** The area under any velocity–time graph gives the total path length, even when the velocity changes sign.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: Δv = ∫a dt. R is false: the signed area gives the displacement; areas below the axis count negative, so path length needs the unsigned areas — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A car starts from rest on a straight road. Its acceleration is 2.0 m/s² for the first 5.0 s and then 1.0 m/s² for the next 6.0 s. Using the area under the acceleration–time graph, find its speed at the end of the 11 s, in m/s.
questions.solution_md: Change in velocity = area under the a–t graph $= 2 \times 5 + 1 \times 6 = 10 + 6 = 16$ m/s. Starting from rest, the speed is $16$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: A walker’s position–time graph is made of three straight pieces: from x = 0 at t = 0 to x = 60 m at t = 20 s, flat until t = 35 s, then back to x = 0 at t = 65 s. Find her average speed over the whole 65 s, in m/s (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Path length $= 60 + 60 = 120$ m (out and back; the flat part adds nothing). Average speed $= \dfrac{120}{65} \approx 1.85$ m/s. (Her average velocity is zero: she returns to the start.)

questions.stem_md: True or false? The area between the velocity–time graph and the time axis of a body that moves forward and then backward along a line always equals the total path length it has covered.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The area gives the displacement when areas below the axis (backward motion) are counted negative; the path length is the sum of the unsigned areas.

questions.stem_md: From the slope of a position–time graph, how can you tell whether a body is moving in the positive or the negative direction, and whether it is speeding up?

answer.model_answer_md: The slope of an x–t graph is the **velocity**: a **positive** slope means motion along +x and a **negative** slope motion along −x. If the slope becomes **steeper** with time (in magnitude), the speed is increasing, so the body is speeding up; if the slope flattens, it is slowing down.

questions.solution_md: Sign of slope; change in steepness.

marking_scheme.step: Steeper: speeding up; flatter: slowing down

questions.stem_md: When a velocity–time graph crosses the time axis, why is the area below the axis taken as negative for the displacement but positive for the path length?

answer.model_answer_md: Below the axis the velocity is **negative**, so that part of the motion is **backward** and subtracts from the displacement, which is a signed quantity. The path length counts the **total distance travelled** regardless of direction, so the areas above and below the axis are added without signs.

questions.solution_md: Displacement is signed; path length is not.

marking_scheme.step: Below the axis v < 0: backward motion reduces the displacement
Path length adds the magnitudes of all areas

questions.stem_md: A ball is thrown vertically upward and caught at the level of release. Describe its velocity–time graph and use it to explain the signs of velocity and acceleration and why the total displacement is zero.

answer.model_answer_md: Taking up as positive, the graph is a **single straight line** of slope −g, starting at +u, crossing zero at the top, and ending at −u. The acceleration is **negative throughout**, while the velocity is positive on the way up and negative on the way down. The two triangles, above and below the axis, have **equal areas**, so the signed area, the displacement, is **zero**.

questions.solution_md: Straight line of slope −g; equal areas above and below.

marking_scheme.step: One straight line from +u to −u with slope −g
Velocity positive then negative; acceleration negative throughout
Equal areas above and below: displacement zero

questions.stem_md: (a) Define path length and displacement and say how they differ. (b) A taxi on a straight road goes 5.0 km east in 12 min, waits 3 min at a signal and then goes 2.0 km west in 6 min. For the whole 21 min find (i) the path length, (ii) the displacement, (iii) the average speed and (iv) the magnitude of the average velocity, in km/h where needed. (c) Explain why the average speed is not the mean of the speeds on the separate legs.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Path length** is the total length of the route actually covered; it is a scalar and never negative. **Displacement** is the final position minus the initial position; it is signed and depends only on the end points, so its magnitude is never more than the path length.

(b) Total time $= 12 + 3 + 6 = 21$ min $= 0.350$ h. (i) Path length $= 5 + 2 = 7$ km. (ii) Displacement $= 5 - 2 = 3$ km east. (iii) Average speed $= \dfrac{7}{0.350} = 20.0$ km/h. (iv) Average velocity $= \dfrac{3}{0.350} \approx 8.57$ km/h east.

(c) The speeds on the legs are 25.0 km/h and 20.0 km/h, but the taxi also spends time at rest. Average speed is the **total path divided by the total time**, so each leg counts in proportion to the time spent on it, and the waiting time counts too.

questions.stem_md: The position of a particle moving on the x-axis is x = 2t³ − 15t² + 24t, with x in m and t in s. (a) Obtain expressions for its velocity and acceleration. (b) At what instants is it momentarily at rest, and where is it then? (c) Find its displacement and the path length covered in the first 5.0 s. (d) Find its average velocity and average speed over these 5.0 s. (e) What is its acceleration at each instant of rest?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 6t^2 - 30t + 24$ and $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 12t - 30$.

(b) $v = 6(t-1)(t-4) = 0$ at $t = 1$ s and $t = 4$ s. There $x(1) = 11$ m and $x(4) = -16$ m.

(c) $x(0) = 0$ and $x(5) = -5$ m, so the displacement is $-5$ m. The path length is $11 + 27 + 11 = 49$ m (forward 11 m, back 27 m, forward 11 m).

(d) $\bar v = \dfrac{-5}{5} = -1.0$ m/s; average speed $= \dfrac{49}{5} = 9.8$ m/s.

(e) $a(1) = 12 \times 1 - 30 = -18$ m/s$^2$ and $a(4) = 12 \times 4 - 30 = 18$ m/s$^2$.

questions.stem_md: (a) For a body moving with constant acceleration, derive v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² using the velocity–time graph. (b) Derive v² = u² + 2as. (c) A train running at 36 km/h accelerates uniformly at 0.50 m/s² for 20 s. Find its final speed in m/s and in km/h, and the distance covered in this time.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The v–t graph is a straight line from $u$ to $v$. Its slope is $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, so $v = u + at$. The area under it is the displacement: rectangle $ut$ plus triangle $\tfrac{1}{2}(v - u)t$, and $v - u = at$, so $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

(b) From $v = u + at$, $t = \dfrac{v - u}{a}$; put in $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ to get $2as = v^2 - u^2$, that is $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

(c) $u = 36$ km/h $= 10$ m/s. $v = u + at = 10 + 0.5 \times 20 = 20$ m/s $= 72$ km/h. $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 10 \times 20 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 400 = 300$ m.

questions.stem_md: A stone is thrown vertically upward at 14.7 m/s from a bridge that is 30 m above the water of a river. Take g = 9.8 m/s² and neglect air resistance. Find (a) the greatest height above the bridge that the stone reaches, (b) the time after which it is back at the level of the bridge and its velocity then, (c) its speed as it reaches the water and (d) the total time from the throw until it hits the water.

answer.model_answer_md:
Take up as positive, $a = -g$.

(a) At the top $v = 0$: $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g} = \dfrac{216.09}{19.6} \approx 11.0$ m above the bridge.

(b) Rise time $= \dfrac{u}{g} = 1.5$ s, so the stone is back at bridge level after $3$ s, moving down at $14.7$ m/s.

(c) From the bridge level downward 30 m: $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh = 216.09 + 2 \times 9.8 \times 30 = 804.09$, so $v = \sqrt{804.09} \approx 28.4$ m/s.

(d) After returning to the bridge level it takes $\dfrac{28.36 - 14.7}{9.8} \approx 1.39$ s more, so the total time is $3 + 1.39 \approx 4.39$ s.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Slopes: stage 1 $a = \dfrac{24}{120} = 0.20$ m/s$^2$; stage 2 $a = 0$; stage 3 $a = \dfrac{0 - 24}{80} = -0.30$ m/s$^2$.

(c) Total time $= 120 + 300 + 80 = 500$ s, so average speed $= \dfrac{9600}{500} = 19.2$ m/s.

(d) Stage 1: a parabola curving upward (slope increasing from zero); stage 2: a straight sloping line (slope 24 m/s); stage 3: a parabola flattening to zero slope at the second station.
